clinicalPearls: Diabetic foot ulcers arise from the interplay of peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease and susceptibility to infection, and are a leading cause of non-traumatic lower-limb amputation

Ulcers are broadly neuropathic, ischaemic or mixed neuroischaemic; neuropathic ulcers form at plantar pressure points with surrounding callus, whereas ischaemic ulcers affect the margins, toes and heel
Loss of protective sensation, foot deformity, high plantar pressures, callus and previous ulceration or amputation are major risk factors, and structured screening stratifies future risk
Infection is a clinical diagnosis and may be limb- and life-threatening; deep infection, abscess and osteomyelitis are common and their usual signs can be muted by neuropathy and ischaemia
The ability to probe to bone, or a large or long-standing ulcer, raises the likelihood of osteomyelitis, and imaging with plain film then MRI, and where needed bone biopsy, helps confirm it
Assessment must include perfusion through pulses, ankle-brachial and toe pressures and duplex, as ischaemia impairs healing and mandates vascular assessment for revascularisation

Management is delivered by a multidisciplinary diabetic foot team and combines offloading, debridement, infection control with appropriate antibiotics, revascularisation where indicated, glycaemic optimisation and wound care
Prevention through education, regular podiatry, appropriate footwear and prompt presentation is central to reducing recurrence and amputation
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic hyperglycaemia drives peripheral neuropathy affecting sensory, motor and autonomic fibres and accelerates atherosclerosis of the leg and foot arteries. Sensory loss removes protective pain, motor neuropathy deforms the foot and concentrates pressure on prominences, and autonomic dysfunction produces dry, fissured skin and arteriovenous shunting. Superimposed arterial disease reduces perfusion and healing capacity. In this setting minor trauma at high-pressure sites goes unnoticed and fails to heal, while impaired neutrophil function and the metabolic effects of hyperglycaemia predispose to rapidly spreading soft-tissue and bone infection, so a superficial ulcer can progress swiftly to a limb-threatening problem.
additionalDifferentials: Neuropathic ulcer from a non-diabetic cause
Acute gout or another inflammatory foot lesion
Malignant ulcer such as a Marjolin ulcer
additionalInvestigations: Structured foot assessment with a monofilament and palpation of pulses
Ankle-brachial and toe pressures with arterial duplex
Plain radiograph and MRI for osteomyelitis or Charcot changes
Deep tissue or bone culture rather than a superficial swab to guide antibiotics
Inflammatory markers and glycaemic assessment including glucose and glycated haemoglobin
Blood cultures if the patient is systemically unwell
redFlags: Spreading cellulitis, abscess, wet gangrene or systemic sepsis
Suspected osteomyelitis with the ability to probe to bone or a chronic non-healing ulcer
Critical limb ischaemia with rest pain, dependent rubor or gangrene
An unexplained warm, swollen foot suggesting Charcot neuroarthropathy
reference.prognosis: Outcomes vary with ulcer depth, infection and ischaemia; many ulcers heal with prompt multidisciplinary care, but recurrence is frequent and an infected, ischaemic ulcer carries a high risk of amputation and mortality.
pitfalls: Relying on superficial swabs rather than deep tissue or bone samples
Missing underlying osteomyelitis or significant ischaemia
Underestimating infection because neuropathy and ischaemia mask the usual signs
Providing inadequate offloading, or delaying vascular or surgical referral
Over-relying on an ankle-brachial index that may be falsely elevated in calcified vessels
references: International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot (IWGDF) guidelines
NICE guidance on diabetic foot problems: prevention and management
IDSA guidance on the diagnosis and treatment of diabetic foot infections
management: Offload plantar pressure with total-contact casting, removable offloading devices or therapeutic footwear to relieve the high-pressure points that drive neuropathic ulceration
Provide structured wound care with regular sharp debridement of callus and non-viable tissue, appropriate dressings and moisture balance
Assess perfusion with pulses, ankle-brachial and toe pressures and duplex, and refer ischaemic or neuroischaemic ulcers for revascularisation
Optimise glycaemic control and modify cardiovascular risk factors to aid healing
Treat superimposed infection promptly with debridement and antibiotics guided by deep tissue culture, and image for osteomyelitis where bone is probed
Manage within a multidisciplinary foot service spanning podiatry, vascular surgery, diabetology and orthotics
Prevent recurrence through structured screening, patient foot-care education, callus care and protective footwear
